blocks.content: 1. Introduction

You know that feeling when your laundry basket is overflowing at the end of the week? You could wash every item the second it gets dirty. Instead most of us let it pile up and do one big load on the weekend.
That is basically the entire batch versus stream decision, shrunk down to one everyday habit. Collect everything and process it all together, or handle each thing the moment it shows up.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396320446-708405677.png
blocks.alt: Raw events splitting into a batch job that returns a result tomorrow versus a stream job that returns a result in seconds

blocks.content: Every data system that moves information from one place to another has to pick one of these two philosophies, or some blend of both. Get it wrong and you either burn a pile of infrastructure money processing things instantly that could have easily waited, or you build a system too slow for what your users actually need.
Batch processing waits for data to pile up, then processes the whole chunk in one go. Stream processing processes each piece of data the moment it shows up, continuously.
1.1 What This Topic Covers
By the end of this you should be able to look at any workload, a nightly report, a fraud check, a live dashboard, and immediately know whether it wants batch, streaming, or something in between.

blocks.content: 2. What Is Batch Processing
Batch processing means you collect data over a period of time, then process the whole accumulated chunk at once, usually on a fixed schedule.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396320446-747400295.png
blocks.alt: Orders accumulating all day, then a nightly job running once and producing a full report

blocks.content: Think of a nightly job that processes yesterday's orders. Nothing happens the instant an order is placed. The order just sits in a table, along with every other order from that day. Then, once a day, a job wakes up, grabs the entire pile, and works through it.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: If a batch job fails partway through, you usually do not get a partial answer. You wait for the next scheduled run, or you rerun the whole batch. That delay is baked into the design, not a bug.
2.1 How A Batch Job Actually Runs
blocks.text: 2.1 How A Batch Job Actually Runs

blocks.content: A batch job almost always follows the same shape, no matter what tool runs it.

["A schedule fires, a cron entry, an Airflow DAG, whatever your team uses","The job reads the full accumulated dataset for the window, say all of yesterday's orders","It processes that entire chunk in one pass, sums, joins, aggregations, whatever the logic needs","It writes the output somewhere, a report table, a file, a dashboard refresh","It shuts down and waits for the next scheduled run"]
items: A schedule fires, a cron entry, an Airflow DAG, whatever your team uses
The job reads the full accumulated dataset for the window, say all of yesterday's orders
It processes that entire chunk in one pass, sums, joins, aggregations, whatever the logic needs
It writes the output somewhere, a report table, a file, a dashboard refresh
It shuts down and waits for the next scheduled run

blocks.content: Nobody is waiting on the other end of a batch job in real time. That is the whole point. It trades immediacy for simplicity and efficiency.
3. What Is Stream Processing
Stream processing means you process each event individually and continuously as it arrives, instead of waiting for a pile to build up. Results are typically available within seconds, sometimes less.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396320447-379410198.png
blocks.alt: An order event hitting a stream, being processed instantly, and producing a result in seconds

blocks.content: There is no yesterday in stream processing. There is only right now. The moment an order gets placed, it becomes an event on a stream, and something is already reading it, checking it, reacting to it.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: Stream processing does not mean faster batch processing. It is a fundamentally different processing model, one event at a time, running forever, not a job that starts and finishes.
3.1 How A Stream Job Actually Runs
blocks.text: 3.1 How A Stream Job Actually Runs

blocks.content: ["An event is produced the instant something happens, an order placed, a click, a sensor reading","A consumer picks it up off the stream almost immediately","The event is processed on its own, maybe joined with recent state, maybe scored against rules","A result is emitted right away, an alert, an update, a write to a live dashboard","The job never stops. It just keeps consuming the next event, forever"]

A consumer picks it up off the stream almost immediately
The event is processed on its own, maybe joined with recent state, maybe scored against rules
A result is emitted right away, an alert, an update, a write to a live dashboard
The job never stops. It just keeps consuming the next event, forever

blocks.content: 4. Latency: Hours Versus Seconds
The single biggest practical difference between the two is latency, how long you wait between something happening and knowing about it.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396320447-173302286.png
blocks.alt: Batch job producing a result hours later compared to a stream job producing a result seconds later

blocks.content: A batch job that runs once a night has latency measured in hours, by design. Even if the processing itself takes two minutes, you are still waiting for the next scheduled window. A stream job has latency measured in seconds, sometimes less, because it reacts the moment an event shows up.

That gap in latency is not an accident or a limitation someone forgot to fix. It comes directly from the shape of each system. Batch is efficient precisely because it processes many records together, spreading fixed overhead across a big pile. Streaming gives up that per record efficiency to react instantly instead.
5. Why Choose One Over The Other
blocks.text: 5. Why Choose One Over The Other

blocks.content: Neither approach is better in general. The right choice depends entirely on whether your workload can tolerate waiting.
5.1 When Batch Is The Right Call
blocks.text: 5.1 When Batch Is The Right Call

blocks.content: Batch is simpler to build, simpler to operate, and more efficient per record, since it processes many rows together instead of one at a time. Choose it whenever the result can wait, and most results can.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396320448-534206959.png
blocks.alt: A daily report that can wait hours, making batch the simpler choice

blocks.content: ["Daily or weekly sales reports","Monthly billing runs","Nightly data warehouse loads","Payroll processing"]

blocks.content: 5.2 When Streaming Is Worth The Complexity
blocks.text: 5.2 When Streaming Is Worth The Complexity

blocks.content: Streaming earns its extra operational cost when low latency actually matters, when a delay of even a few minutes defeats the purpose of the system entirely.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396320448-277180419.png
blocks.alt: A fraud attempt that needs action right now, making a stream job the right catch

blocks.content: ["Fraud detection, where you want to block a bad transaction before it clears","Live dashboards, where a stale number an hour old is useless","Real time recommendations while a user is still browsing","Monitoring and alerting, where you want to know a server is down within seconds, not tomorrow morning"]
items: Fraud detection, where you want to block a bad transaction before it clears
Live dashboards, where a stale number an hour old is useless
Real time recommendations while a user is still browsing
Monitoring and alerting, where you want to know a server is down within seconds, not tomorrow morning

blocks.content: 6. The Trade Offs
Once you look past latency, batch and stream systems differ in ways that show up mostly when things go wrong or get weird, not on a calm, happy path day.
6.1 Operational Complexity

A batch job is a process that starts, does its work, and stops. If it crashes, you fix the bug and rerun it tomorrow. A streaming system never stops. It is always on infrastructure, which means it needs monitoring, alerting, autoscaling, and careful capacity planning around traffic spikes, all running continuously.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: Teams sometimes underestimate this. Running a streaming pipeline is closer to running a production API than running a scheduled script. Budget the on call effort accordingly.
6.2 Out Of Order And Late Arriving Events
blocks.text: 6.2 Out Of Order And Late Arriving Events

blocks.content: In a batch job, ordering barely matters. You have the entire chunk of data sitting in front of you before you start, so you can sort it however you like. In a stream, events can arrive late or out of order, a mobile client goes offline and reconnects, a network hiccup delays a message by a few seconds.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396320448-454265462.png
blocks.alt: An event generated at 10:00 that gets delayed by the network and only arrives at 10:05, forcing the stream to reorder it

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: Streaming systems handle this with windowing and watermarks, essentially a grace period for how late an event is allowed to be before it gets dropped or counted separately. Get the grace period wrong and you either wait forever or silently lose data.
6.3 Exactness Versus Speed

Streaming systems often trade off perfect exactness for speed. A batch job can afford to process every record exactly once, carefully, because it has all the time in the world within its scheduled window. A streaming system under load sometimes settles for at least once delivery, meaning a record might get counted twice under rare failure conditions, in exchange for never blocking the pipeline.

This is a real design decision, not a flaw. Exactly once streaming semantics exist and tools like Kafka and Flink support them, but they add coordination overhead. Many streaming use cases, like a live view counter, are fine with an approximate number that is almost always right, updated instantly, rather than a perfect number that is always a few minutes stale.

7. Micro Batching: The Middle Ground
Micro batching is a compromise. Instead of waiting a full day, you process small batches very frequently, every few seconds, and each of those tiny batches runs through a normal batch engine.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396321441-503766783.png
blocks.alt: Events arriving continuously, grouped into a small batch every few seconds, and processed like a tiny batch job to feel like streaming

blocks.content: It is not true event by event processing. It is many, many small batch jobs running back to back, fast enough that from the outside it feels close to real time.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: Micro batching still has a latency floor equal to the batch interval. If your interval is two seconds, no result can ever arrive faster than two seconds, even for the simplest event. True streaming engines do not have that floor.
7.1 How Spark Streaming Did This

The original Spark Streaming model, before Spark added a proper continuous streaming engine, worked exactly this way. It sliced an incoming stream into tiny time windows, often around one second, and ran each window through Spark's regular batch engine. This let one team reuse the same batch processing code and mental model for something that looked and felt like streaming, without building a separate streaming runtime from scratch.
8. Real Systems You Will Actually Use
blocks.text: 8. Real Systems You Will Actually Use

blocks.content: These ideas are not just theory. Specific tools exist for each side, and knowing the names helps in interviews and in real architecture discussions.
8.1 The Batch Toolbox

Hadoop MapReduce was the original large scale batch engine, splitting a huge dataset across many machines, mapping, shuffling, and reducing it down. Apache Spark improved on this with an in memory model, making batch jobs that used to take hours run in minutes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396321443-397544333.png
blocks.alt: Hadoop MapReduce and Apache Spark both feeding into batch processing

blocks.content: 8.2 The Streaming Toolbox

Kafka Streams is a lightweight library for processing events straight out of Kafka topics inside your own application. Apache Flink is a full streaming engine built for continuous, low latency processing with strong exactly once guarantees. Spark Streaming is Spark's streaming layer, historically micro batch based, now also supporting a more continuous mode.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396321443-101496933.png
blocks.alt: Kafka Streams, Apache Flink, and Spark Streaming all feeding into stream processing

blocks.content: 9. Worked Example: One Company, Two Pipelines
blocks.text: 9. Worked Example: One Company, Two Pipelines

blocks.content: Picture an e commerce company. Every order placed on the site generates the same underlying event, an order record with a customer, an amount, and a timestamp. That single stream of order data feeds two completely different pipelines, because two completely different questions need answers on two completely different timelines.
9.1 The Nightly Sales Report

Every night at 2 AM, a batch job wakes up, pulls every order from the previous day, groups them by category and region, and emails a sales summary to the leadership team. Nobody needs this report at 2:03 AM. They need it by the time they check their inbox in the morning. Batch is the obvious, cheap, simple choice here.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396321444-61336214.png
blocks.alt: Orders table feeding a nightly batch job that produces a sales report email

blocks.content: 9.2 The Real Time Fraud Check

At the exact same time, every single order also flows into a fraud detection stream. A rules engine checks each order the instant it is placed, unusual amount, unusual location, a card that failed three times in the last minute, and either lets it through or flags it for review within a second or two. Waiting until the nightly batch job to catch fraud would mean the money is already gone by the time anyone notices.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396321445-656163298.png
blocks.alt: Order stream feeding a fraud rules engine that blocks or flags suspicious orders instantly

blocks.title: Same Data, Two Timelines
blocks.text: The nightly report and the fraud check read from the same order data. One can comfortably wait until morning. The other has to react within seconds. That is the whole batch versus stream decision playing out on a single dataset, inside one company.

blocks.content: 10. Implementation: Both Sides Of The Fence
blocks.text: 10. Implementation: Both Sides Of The Fence

blocks.content: Seeing actual code for both sides makes the difference concrete. Here is a simplified version of each pipeline from the e commerce example above.
10.1 A Simple Batch Job
This job runs once, on a schedule, reads every order from yesterday, and writes a summary. It does not care about individual orders arriving in real time, it just wants the full pile.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: Notice there is no loop waiting on new orders. The job runs, queries the whole window, produces one output, and exits. If it dies halfway, you rerun the whole thing tomorrow, no partial state to reconcile.
10.2 A Simple Stream Consumer
This consumer never stops. It sits on a Kafka topic and reacts to each order the instant it shows up, scoring it for fraud within milliseconds.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.content: In production you would also track consumer offsets and checkpoint progress, so if this process restarts it resumes from the last event it actually processed, instead of skipping events or reprocessing the entire topic from scratch.
11. The Interview Angle

In a system design interview, the batch versus stream question rarely gets asked directly. It shows up disguised inside a bigger design, and the interviewer is watching whether you default to streaming everywhere out of habit, or actually reason about each workload.
11.1 Do Not Default To Streaming Everywhere
blocks.text: 11.1 Do Not Default To Streaming Everywhere

blocks.content: Streaming sounds impressive, so candidates sometimes reach for Kafka and Flink for every single requirement in a design, even the ones that are clearly fine waiting until tomorrow. That adds unnecessary operational complexity, more moving parts, more monitoring, more ways for the system to break, for zero real benefit.

["Ask yourself, does this specific requirement actually need an answer within seconds?","If the answer can wait minutes or hours without hurting anyone, say so out loud, and default to batch","Reserve streaming for the requirements that genuinely cannot tolerate delay, fraud, live pricing, safety alerts","It is completely fine, and often correct, for one design to use both batch and streaming for different parts"]
items: Ask yourself, does this specific requirement actually need an answer within seconds?
If the answer can wait minutes or hours without hurting anyone, say so out loud, and default to batch
Reserve streaming for the requirements that genuinely cannot tolerate delay, fraud, live pricing, safety alerts
It is completely fine, and often correct, for one design to use both batch and streaming for different parts

blocks.content: A senior engineer does not reach for the fanciest tool. They match the tool to how fast the answer actually needs to arrive.
